title: A Houston Desi Supermarket Got Filmed by a GOP Congressional Candidate — and the Owner's Response Was Quietly Devastating
excerpt: Sangam Supermarket's food-storage practices went viral on social media, but the real story is what happens when culture-war content creators target NRI small businesses that have quietly served communities for decades.
body:
The videos were textbook outrage bait. Nick Plumb, a Texas Republican who once ran for Congress, drove to Sangam Supermarket in north Houston on consecutive days in mid-May, filming boxes of produce and packaged goods stacked on the asphalt outside the store — wedged, as he noted with evident disgust, between two sets of dumpsters.

"Check out the third-world standards straight from the back alleys of India," Plumb wrote, attaching footage that racked up hundreds of thousands of views. "This has ZERO place in American grocery stores."

Plumb's visits to Sangam sit within a broader pattern that Indian-American business owners in Texas have been tracking with growing alarm. A wave of American influencers and content creators has been targeting Indian-owned establishments across the state, filming perceived violations and packaging them for social media audiences primed by anti-immigration rhetoric. The grocery store genre — with its unfamiliar produce, its different packaging, its sometimes improvised storage during high-volume sales — has proved especially lucrative for engagement.

## What Actually Happened at Sangam

The store's owner, who has lived in the United States for 35 years and built Sangam into one of Houston's established South Asian supermarkets, eventually came outside to talk to Plumb. The conversation, also recorded and posted, is worth watching in full for what it reveals about the impossible position NRI entrepreneurs now occupy.

The owner was neither defensive nor confrontational. He told Plumb he had watched all the videos. He acknowledged the products had been outside — a large shipment during a sale, not enough warehouse space, moved indoors by evening. He said if a health inspector ordered him to dispose of the goods, he would comply without argument. "I never back out of problems," he said.

Then came the detail that complicated Plumb's narrative. The owner said he had voted for President Trump in the last election. He said he opposed illegal immigration. He was, in other words, precisely the kind of legal immigrant, long-established business owner, and Republican voter that the party's mainstream rhetoric claims to champion — and yet here was a fellow Republican with a camera treating his livelihood as content.

## The Bigger Picture for Desi Grocery Stores

For the roughly 5,500 Indian-owned grocery stores operating across the United States, the Sangam episode lands in an environment that was already hostile. The Federation of Indian Associations has documented a rise in harassment incidents targeting South Asian businesses since 2024, with grocery stores and restaurants disproportionately affected.

The food-safety dimension is not entirely manufactured. American health codes are specific about outdoor storage, temperature control, and pest exposure. Stores that unload shipments onto parking lots during sales — a practice common in wholesale and ethnic grocery retail — do technically create inspection vulnerabilities. But the way these violations are filmed, framed, and distributed online bears no resemblance to an actual food-safety complaint process. It is performance, not regulation.

"There is a difference between calling the health department and calling your followers," said Ravi Mehta, a Houston-based immigration attorney who advises small-business owners. "One gets the problem fixed. The other gets the business destroyed."

## What NRIs Who Run Small Businesses Should Know

Industry groups have been circulating updated guidance for desi grocery store owners in the wake of viral incidents. Key recommendations include: never unload perishable goods onto uncovered pavement, even temporarily; install security cameras covering loading areas; document compliance with health inspectors proactively; and prepare employees for encounters with people filming in or around the store.

The Texas Department of State Health Services confirms that food establishments may be inspected at any time and that complaints can be filed by anyone. Store owners who maintain clean documentation and inspection histories have legal standing to challenge defamatory social media content, though the practical cost of doing so remains prohibitive for most small businesses.

## The Diaspora Dimension

For NRIs who have spent decades building businesses in the United States, the Sangam story carries a particular sting. The owner did everything the assimilation playbook prescribes — three and a half decades of residency, a business that employs local workers, civic participation, even alignment with the governing party's immigration stance. None of it insulated him from becoming content.

The question now facing the broader desi business community is whether the current wave of targeted filming will peak and recede, as previous cycles of anti-immigrant social media campaigns have, or whether it represents a more durable shift in how Indian-owned establishments are treated in the public discourse.

Plumb, for his part, invited the Sangam owner to update him in two days. Whether the follow-up video will show a clean store or serve as another episode in the series remains to be seen. The owner, characteristically, said he would be ready either way.
